title: AVL Trees
summary: Keeping a search tree balanced - the AVL balance condition and why it bounds the height by about 1.44 log n, storing heights in the nodes, left and right rotations, the four imbalance cases (left-left, right-right, left-right, right-left), insertion with rebalancing on the way back up, deletion, and how AVL trees compare with red-black trees, treaps and B-trees.

cards.q: Which balance factors are allowed in an AVL tree?
cards.a:
-1, 0 and +1

The two subtrees of every node may differ in height by at most one.

cards.q: A node has balance +2 and its left child has balance -1. What fixes it?
cards.a:
Rotate the child left, then the node right

This is the left-right case: the double rotation straightens the zig-zag first.

cards.q: Why does a rotation keep the tree a valid binary search tree?
cards.a:
It keeps the in-order sequence of keys the same

A x B y C reads the same before and after a rotation at y.
